title: Ship your interpreter, explained
h1: Ship your interpreter: a proof that a compiled C interpreter's RISC-V binary implements its language's semantics
lead: Kiran Gopinathan's project proves, in Lean 4, a theorem about the shipped binary of a small interpreter written in C. Start the RISC-V machine (the Sail ISA model) at the interpreter's interp_run, with a WHILE program's AST in memory. Then it halts with exit code 0 and output out exactly when the program's big-step semantics gives out, and if it runs forever the program has no result. No C semantics or compiler is trusted. What is trusted: the Sail model, the ELF's bytes, the loading hypothesis (which assumes the parser already ran and that heap and stack suffice) and the semantics itself.
desc: An unofficial plain-English roadmap of Basis Research's ship-your-interpreter: a Lean 4 proof, through an Iris program logic over the Sail RISC-V model, that a compiled C interpreter's ELF implements a big-step semantics of WHILE.
startNote: Read the headline endToEnd_refinement, then the Roadmap, which walks the proof from the WHILE semantics and the RISC-V model, through the memory layout and the Iris program logic, to the theorem. For the boundaries, see Loaded (what is assumed) and Trust.
sizeNote: About 175,700 lines of project Lean in 822 files (Vsa/ about 66,000, VsaIris/ about 109,400), plus about 246,000 lines of vendored, mostly generated Sail RISC-V model in riscv-lean/ (not scanned here).
agentCtx: ship-your-interpreter (Basis Research, Kiran Gopinathan): a Lean 4 proof that the RV64 ELF of a WHILE interpreter written in C, run on the Sail-generated RISC-V model from the entry of interp_run, refines an inductive big-step semantics of WHILE; built with an Iris-style machine program logic.

gloss.String: Text. Program output is a string: everything print and println wrote, or the machine's console contents.
gloss.Nat: The natural numbers 0, 1, 2, …. Exit codes, addresses and step counters are natural numbers.
